title: Parliament Voted Against Chat Control. It Passed Anyway.
summary: On 9 July 2026, 314 European Parliament members — a clear simple majority — voted to reject the Chat Control 1.0 ePrivacy derogation. Under EU second-reading rules, a simple majority wasn't enough: blocking the measure required an absolute majority of roughly 360 of the 720 MEPs, and the opposition fell more than 40 votes short. The voluntary message-scanning regime now runs until 3 April 2028.
body:
The mechanism matters more than the margin.

On 9 July 2026, the European Parliament voted on a motion to reject the Chat Control 1.0 derogation extension. Three hundred and fourteen MEPs backed rejection. Two hundred and seventy-six opposed it. Seventeen abstained. Under normal democratic accounting, 314 to 276 is a clean majority. Under EU second-reading rules, it is a defeat: blocking a measure at second reading requires an absolute majority — roughly 360 of the Parliament's 720 members. The opposition fell more than 40 votes short.

A second vote followed, on an amended position that included a Renew group carve-out formally excluding end-to-end encrypted communications. On that vote the numbers inverted: 276 MEPs supported the amended text, 286 opposed it, 30 abstained. The amended text now advances to the Council.

The derogation runs until 3 April 2028.

**What the law does**

Chat Control 1.0 is a temporary exception to the EU's ePrivacy Directive. It permits platforms — including Meta's WhatsApp and Messenger — to voluntarily scan private messages and direct communications for known child sexual abuse material. The scanning is not mandatory. It does not require a warrant or specific suspicion of wrongdoing. End-to-end encrypted services are formally exempt under the amendment adopted in the same session, though critics have characterised that exemption as largely symbolic.

The regulation was introduced as a transitional measure to bridge the gap while EU legislators negotiated a permanent framework — Chat Control 2.0, which has stalled over privacy and legal objections. The temporary measure expired on 3 April 2026. Parliament voted in March to reject renewal, 311 to 228 (92 abstentions). That should have been the end of it.

**The procedural revival**

It wasn't.

In late June, Parliament President Roberta Metsola reintroduced the measure at the request of the European People's Party (EPP) and member states. On 8 July, Parliament approved an urgency motion — 331 to 304 — placing the text back before plenary before the summer recess. The EPP framing: Parliament should not allow the voluntary scanning framework to lapse while child protection legislation remained unfinished.

**Who said what**

Patrick Breyer, the former Pirate Party MEP who has sustained opposition to the measure across multiple legislative cycles: "The fact that Chat Control is moving forward against the will of the majority of voting MEPs is a farce and damages democracy."

German MEP Svenja Hahn said the measure "opens the door for mass surveillance of all private communication."

Greens/EFA MEP Ignazio Marino: "Children are protected by smart enforcement, not by scanning the private messages of millions of innocent people."

Pirate MEP Markéta Gregorová put the vote in procedural terms: "Usually, when the Parliament rejects a text, the Council stops working on it and the Commission eventually withdraws it. Now, we are forced into a second vote that questions the essence of democracy."

**What comes next**

The amended text advances to the Council. Legislators now have until 3 April 2028 to renew it, let it lapse, or replace it with a permanent Chat Control 2.0 framework. The 2.0 proposal — which would extend mandatory scanning to encrypted communications — remains contested. Its trajectory is separate from this extension vote.

The July procedural maneuver bought time. Whether that time produces a substantive resolution or another extension is a different question.
